# Worksheet: Correlation and Linear Regression

[📥 Booby data](data/booby_aggression.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="booby_aggression.csv"} [📥 Rope trick data](data/rope_trick.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="rope_trick.csv"} [📥 Lion data](data/lion_noses.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="lion_noses.csv"} [📥 Tools script (.R)](themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R){.btn .btn-primary download="r_themes_and_functions.R"} [📥 Script skeleton (.R)](data/10_correlation_linear_models.R){.btn .btn-primary download="10_correlation_linear_models.R"}

This worksheet runs in two halves, matching the lecture. **Parts 1–4 are correlation**: two measured variables, one number, no direction. **Parts 5–8 are regression**: a fitted line, the sums of squares it is made of, and the diagnostics that decide whether to believe it.

Three datasets, all from Whitlock & Schluter:

- `booby_aggression.csv` — Example 16.1. Nestling visits and adult aggression in Nazca boobies
- `rope_trick.csv` — Example 16.5. Years since seeing the Indian rope trick, and how impressive it is remembered as
- `lion_noses.csv` — Example 17.1. Proportion of black on a male lion's nose, and its age

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 1 · Setup and the data

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

booby_df <- read_csv("data/booby_aggression.csv")
rope_df  <- read_csv("data/rope_trick.csv")
lion_df  <- read_csv("data/lion_noses.csv")

booby_df
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2 · Correlation

**▶ Run this** — look at the data before you test it:

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · Correlation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(booby_df, aes(visits_as_nestling, future_aggression)) +
  geom_point()
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Is the trend straight, or is there a curve in it? Any point far off on its own?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

**▶ Run this** — the coefficient, then the test:

``` r
# ── Part 2.2 · Correlation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
cor(booby_df$visits_as_nestling, booby_df$future_aggression)

cor.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling, booby_df$future_aggression)
```

**▶ Run this** — square it for the variance explained:

``` r
# ── Part 2.3 · Correlation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
r_booby <- cor(booby_df$visits_as_nestling, booby_df$future_aggression)

r_booby^2
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Fill these in from the output above.

```
r = ____________   p = ____________   r squared = ____________

What share of the variation do the two variables share? ____________ %
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Write one sentence stating what the correlation means biologically — without using the word "cause."

```
____________________________________________________________

____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 3 · Correlation assumptions

Pearson's r assumes both variables are normal, the relationship is linear, and no outlier is driving it.

**▶ Run this** — the formal test on each variable:

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · Correlation assumptions ──────────────────────────────────
shapiro.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling)

shapiro.test(booby_df$future_aggression)
```

**▶ Run this** — and the picture:

``` r
# ── Part 3.2 · Correlation assumptions ──────────────────────────────────
h1 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(visits_as_nestling)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10)
h2 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(future_aggression)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10)
q1 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(sample = visits_as_nestling)) + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()
q2 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(sample = future_aggression)) + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()

(h1 / h2) | (q1 / q2)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Remember H₀ here is "these data ARE normal." Do both variables pass?

```
visits: p = __________ pass? ______    aggression: p = __________ pass? ______
```

✏️ **Your turn:** One of them lands very close to 0.05 while its QQ plot looks fine. At n = 24, which do you believe, and does it change the coefficient you report?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 4 · When normality fails

Same workflow, a dataset that does not cooperate: an impressiveness **score**, which is bounded and lumpy.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · When normality fails ─────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(rope_df, aes(years_since_seen, impressiveness)) +
  geom_point()

shapiro.test(rope_df$impressiveness)
```

**▶ Run this** — both coefficients on the same data:

``` r
# ── Part 4.2 · When normality fails ─────────────────────────────────────
cor.test(rope_df$years_since_seen, rope_df$impressiveness)

cor.test(rope_df$years_since_seen, rope_df$impressiveness,
         method = "spearman")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which coefficient do you report for these data, and why?

```
Pearson r = __________   Spearman rho = __________

I report ______________ because ______________________________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Spearman works on ranks. What did you give up by switching to it?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

**That is the correlation half.** The rest of the worksheet fits a line.

# Part 5 · Fitting a regression

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Fitting a regression ─────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(lion_df, aes(proportion_black, age_years)) +
  geom_point()

lion_model <- lm(age_years ~ proportion_black, data = lion_df)

summary(lion_model)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Write the fitted equation, then the slope as a sentence in the units of the data.

```
age = ____________ + ____________ x proportion_black

For every 0.1 more black on the nose, predicted age goes up by ______ years.
```

✏️ **Your turn:** The intercept is the predicted age at `proportion_black = 0`. The youngest lion measured was 1.1 years old. Is the intercept a statement about newborn lions? Why not?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

**▶ Run this** — the line with its confidence band:

``` r
# ── Part 5.2 · Fitting a regression ─────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(lion_df, aes(proportion_black, age_years)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

**▶ Run this** — predict a lion with a half-black nose, two ways:

``` r
# ── Part 5.3 · Fitting a regression ─────────────────────────────────────
new_lion <- tibble(proportion_black = 0.50)

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "confidence")

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "prediction")
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which interval is wider, and what question does each one answer?

```
____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 6 · Sums of squares

The lecture's centrepiece: build the partition yourself, then let R hand you the same numbers.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 6.1 · Sums of squares ──────────────────────────────────────────
fitted_age <- predict(lion_model)
mean_age   <- mean(lion_df$age_years)

ss_total <- sum((lion_df$age_years - mean_age)^2)
ss_reg   <- sum((fitted_age - mean_age)^2)
ss_resid <- sum((lion_df$age_years - fitted_age)^2)

c(total = ss_total, regression = ss_reg, residual = ss_resid)

ss_reg + ss_resid
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Does the partition add up, and what fraction of the total does the line account for?

```
ss_reg + ss_resid = __________   ss_total = __________

ss_reg / ss_total = __________   Where have you seen that number before? ______
```

**▶ Run this** — the same three numbers from R:

``` r
# ── Part 6.2 · Sums of squares ──────────────────────────────────────────
anova(lion_model)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Match the table to what you computed.

```
Sum Sq, proportion_black row = __________   Sum Sq, Residuals row = __________

Df = ______ and ______      Mean Sq = Sum Sq / ______
```

**▶ Run this** — the t on the slope, squared:

``` r
# ── Part 6.3 · Sums of squares ──────────────────────────────────────────
summary(lion_model)$coefficients

summary(lion_model)$coefficients[2, 3]^2
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Compare that to the F value in the ANOVA table. What does the match tell you about the two tests?

```
t squared = __________   F = __________

____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 7 · Regression assumptions

Every check from here is on the **residuals**, not the raw data.

**▶ Run this** — the four standard diagnostic plots:

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · Regression assumptions ───────────────────────────────────
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lion_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**▶ Run this** — the formal test on the residuals:

``` r
# ── Part 7.2 · Regression assumptions ───────────────────────────────────
shapiro.test(residuals(lion_model))
```

✏️ **Your turn:** One line per assumption. Say what you looked at, not just pass or fail.

```
Linearity (residuals vs fitted): ____________________________

Equal variance (scale-location): ____________________________

Normality (QQ + Shapiro p = ______): ________________________

Influential points (Cook's distance): _______________________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Would you report this model as it stands? One sentence.

```
____________________________________________________________
```

# Part 8 · The figure you hand in

Everything above was for looking. This one is for showing, so it gets the full treatment.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
final_plot <- ggplot(lion_df, aes(proportion_black, age_years)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Nose pigmentation predicts age in male lions",
    subtitle = "Fitted least-squares line with 95% confidence band",
    x = "Proportion of black on nose",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 12)

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/lion_regression.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 6,
  height = 4,
  units  = "in"
)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Open the PDF and check the axis labels are readable before you submit it.

# Review and checkpoint

At this point you can:

- [ ] Run and interpret `cor.test()`, and square r for the variance explained
- [ ] Check correlation assumptions on the raw variables and switch to Spearman when they fail
- [ ] Fit a line with `lm()` and state the slope in the units of the data
- [ ] Build $SS_{regression}$, $SS_{residual}$ and $SS_{total}$ by hand and match them to `anova()`
- [ ] Show that t² = F for a one-predictor model
- [ ] Read the four regression diagnostics off the residuals
- [ ] Export a labelled figure to PDF
